stemMd: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

options.label: A
options.textMd: The factors courts list for deciding whether to overrule a precedent do not determine outcomes, since they carry no weights and most of them presuppose a view about whether the precedent was right; what they do impose is an obligation to justify the decision publicly.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Because the weight to be given to reliance cannot be settled objectively, courts deciding whether to overrule a precedent should confine themselves to the other factors on the list.

options.label: C
options.textMd: A precedent should be overruled whenever the court becomes convinced that it was wrong when it was decided, because the cost of perpetuating an error outweighs the benefits of stability.

options.label: D
options.textMd: A court that changes its mind frequently invites the suspicion that its rulings track the composition of the bench rather than the law.

options.label: E
options.textMd: The doctrine governing when a precedent may be overruled ought to be abandoned, since its criteria cannot be applied without presupposing an answer to the question they were framed to settle.

explanationMd:
A main-point answer must cover the whole arc of the passage and land on the claim the author actually defends — not on the most quotable sentence and not on a position the author merely reports.

Trace the arc:

1. Overruling is governed by a balance between stability and the cost of perpetuating error. (Setup.)
2. Courts list factors to make that balance tractable, and the list "has the look of an instrument for disciplining judgment." (The view under examination.)
3. "It disciplines less than it appears to, for two reasons": the factors carry no weights, and most of them can be assessed only by someone who has already decided whether the precedent was right. (The author's central argument.)
4. "The conclusion to draw is not that the doctrine is empty": it is "a constraint of candour rather than of outcome." (The author's qualification, which he insists on.)

The author speaks in his own voice in paragraphs 3 and 4, and those two paragraphs make one connected claim with two halves: the list does not determine what a court decides, but it does force the court to say publicly why. The choice stating that the factors do not determine outcomes but do impose an obligation to justify publicly states both halves and adds nothing else.

How to check a main-point answer: for each choice, ask (i) does the author ever assert this, and (ii) which paragraph would have to be deleted for it to be the main point? The choice urging that the doctrine be abandoned fails test (i) — paragraph 4 opens by refusing exactly that conclusion. The choice about a court that changes its mind frequently passes (i) but fails (ii): it is one clause of paragraph 1, and paragraphs 2 through 4 would all have to go. The choice recommending overruling whenever the court is convinced the precedent was wrong, and the choice recommending that courts confine themselves to the other factors, both fail (i) outright; the passage recommends no decision procedure at all. Only the choice stating both halves of the author's claim needs every paragraph and asserts nothing the author does not.

distractorRationale.e: This takes the critique of paragraph 3 and pushes it one step further than the author will go. Paragraph 4 begins by refusing precisely this inference — "The conclusion to draw is not that the doctrine is empty" — and then identifies a constraint the doctrine does impose. A main point cannot be a conclusion the passage explicitly declines to draw.
distractorRationale.d: This is a single clause from the opening paragraph, offered there as one item on the stability side of the balance. It is accurate but far too small: it says nothing about the list of factors, nothing about the two difficulties, and nothing about the constraint of candour, so three of the four paragraphs would be left unaccounted for.
distractorRationale.c: The passage never recommends when a precedent should be overruled, and this choice resolves in one direction the very balance the author says the doctrine leaves unresolved. It also reverses paragraph 3's point: if unworkability and reliance cannot be judged without a prior view on correctness, a rule keyed to correctness alone is not a fix but a restatement of the problem.
distractorRationale.b: No such remedy appears anywhere in the passage. The author says reliance judgments smuggle in a view about which expectations the law ought to protect, but he treats that as an illustration of a general difficulty affecting most of the factors, not as a reason to drop one factor and keep the rest — which would leave the other affected factors untouched.

accessibilityText: A main-point question on the four-paragraph passage about the doctrine governing when courts may overrule their own precedents, with five answer choices labelled A through E. No figures, tables or mathematical notation appear in the question or the choices.

review.notes: Each choice was tested against two questions: does the author assert it, and does it require the whole passage? Only (E) passes both. (A) is the closest competitor and is closed by the first sentence of paragraph 4, which refuses that conclusion in so many words; the passage was written with that sentence in place for this reason.
